newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Accused Serb's wife takes stand at warcrimes trial.
newsitem.headline: Accused Serb's wife takes stand at warcrimes trial.

text.p: The wife of an alleged Bosnian Serb murderer and rapist took the stand as a character witness at a U.N. war crimes trial on Tuesday.
Entering the Hague courtroom of the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia, Mira Tadic smiled briefly at her husband, Dusan, who sat in the dock flanked by two U.N. security guards.
Mira Tadic, 35 and dressed in a crisp white suit, answered defence questions for 40 minutes before the session was adjourned until 0800 GMT on Wednesday.

Appearing tense as she gripped the arms of the chair in the witness stand, she gave details of how the couple met in Kozarac in 1976, married three years later and then underwent a "divorce of convenience" in 1987.
U.N. prosecutors accuse Tadic, 41, of murdering, torturing and raping Moslems at Serb-run prison camps during a Serb campaign of "ethnic cleansing" in northwest Bosnia in 1992.
The former bar-owner and karate teacher denies the charges and says he was never at the Omarska camp, one of three where alleged atrocities took place against Moslem prisoners.

Mira Tadic told the court that in 1986 she and Dusan had gone to Libya where she had found a nursing job. On their return to Bosnia in 1987, the couple were "divorced" to make it easier for her to apply for a nursing post in Switzerland.

She told British barrister Steven Kay, defending Tadic, that she did not get the job and that the two had never formally re-married, although they continued to live together as man and wife, raising two daughters, Valentina, 16, and Alexandra, 7.
Petite and dark-haired, Mira Tadic, also a Bosnian Serb, said that both she and Dusan had Moslem and Croat friends in Kozarac before the 3-1/2 year Bosnian conflict erupted in 1992.

Speaking through an interpreter, she said Dusan had worked for several years at a company which assembled electronic appliances, but in 1987 he set up a contracting firm providing carpentry on construction sites.
As she left the courtroom, the two exchanged smiles.

Since his arrest in Germany in February 1994 and transfer to The Hague in April 1995, Tadic has had several visits from his wife. The defendant is one of seven indicted war crimes suspects held at the tribunal's detention centre.
Tadic's trial began in The Hague on May 7 and is expected to end by late-November.

The tribunal has indicted 75 suspects, primarily Serbs, but most remain at large, including the two most prominent: deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and military commander General Ratko Mladic.
